inline.s: Contemplating these six similes is, it is true, contemplating the empty mark of all dharmas — which is precisely contemplating the nature of suchness, because nature and mark are from the first interfused. So by contemplating dependent arising one may enter the unmoving suchness. Hence the nature of the unconditioned Dharma is approached by contemplating the marks of conditioned dharmas as dream and illusion: thus one clings to neither extreme, and so accords with the middle way. This meaning has been discussed in full above.

Let us now explain it again by the three natures and the three non-natures. In the six similes, whichever one simile you take up, the principle of the three natures and three non-natures can be made clear. Here we shall take the general simile of the dream; the rest can be known by the same pattern.

The three natures and the three non-natures are found in the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra and in the various sutras and treatises of the Dharma-characteristics school. They are the essential doctrine of that school. The Buddha set forth dharma-marks precisely in order to make this clear. If one does not know to give it weight, but only dissects minute details — though one may analyze every dharma-mark most exhaustively, one is still counting sand in the ocean and has lost the point of what one follows. You should know that students of the nature school, too, ought to be thoroughly familiar with the meaning of the three natures and three non-natures, for this meaning runs through both nature and marks. If you know it, you can understand dependent arising and the emptiness of nature more thoroughly, and your cultivation of contemplation will be more effective. What was said above about the contemplation of dream is still only a general contemplation of the main point; if one contemplates according to the principle of the three natures and three non-natures, one enters deeper and subtler ground.

What are the three natures? First, the nature of pervasive imagining; second, the nature of dependence on others; third, the nature of perfect accomplishment. Pervasive imagining means universal calculation and clinging. It is what the nature school regularly calls discrimination, clinging, grasping at conditions, ignorance, the deluded mind, deluded thought, and so on. The nature school also calls it the nature of discrimination. This is deluded thought; why call it a nature? The point is to make clear that although it is ignorance and deluded thought, it is nonetheless a transformation of the true mind and does not exist apart from the nature of reality. The Dharma-characteristics school names it the nature of pervasive imagining, speaking only with respect to the stage of ordinary beings; the nature school names it the nature of discrimination, which covers both ordinary and noble. The nature of discrimination at the noble stage means that the noble ones manifest responsively according to conditions and teach according to capacity with not the slightest error; it appears to involve discrimination because it is viewed from the side of living beings, but it does not mean that those at the noble stage still give rise to conceptual discrimination. This should be understood.

The nature of dependence on others is what the nature school calls dependent arising, arising from conditions, and arising from nature. It is precisely the marks and functions that the essential nature brings forth in accord with conditions. Marks and functions are never apart from the nature-essence; without the nature-essence there would be no marks and functions. Hence it is called the nature of dependence on others. To depend on means to follow; others refers to conditions.

As for the nature of perfect accomplishment: perfect means complete, and accomplished means inherently possessed. The words perfect and accomplished are spoken with respect to the essence, making clear that from the first it is complete and fully endowed and is not something manufactured. They also refer to marks and functions, meaning that marks and functions are inherently possessed by the essence, their pure virtues complete. Real means true. This is what the nature school regularly calls the Dharma-realm, suchness, tathatā, the true mind, the mark of reality, perfect enlightenment, the mind of intrinsic purity, and so on — its names are numberless. The nature school also calls it the nature of reality.

What are the three non-natures? First, the mark of no-mark; second, the non-nature of birth; third, the non-nature of the supreme meaning. The word no is very supple: it carries the sense of not, and the sense of emptying, that is, that one must not cling.

As for the mark of no-mark: living beings, in regard to all things, falsely reckon that there is a self and there are dharmas, and cling to them — this is what is called pervasive imagining. They do not realize that the marks of self and the marks of dharmas clung to by pervasive imagining arise entirely from mistaken recognition, as when one takes a rope for a snake. Not only is the snake's mark unreal; the rope's mark too — was it ever truly real? Hence it is called the mark of no-mark: illusory marks are not the nature of reality. One should realize that within the nature there are from the first no marks, and so one should not cling to marks but be without them; that is the nature.

As for the non-nature of birth: birth means birth from conditions. All dharmas merely, by the coming together of causes and conditions, falsely appear as marks of arising — this is what is called dependence on others. Since they are thus born of conditions, it is clear that all dharmas have from the first no substantial reality; their essence is only pure nature. It is just as the arising of a rope also comes about through the gathering of causes and conditions: the rope is not a substantial reality; its substance is hemp. Hence it is called the non-nature of birth: dharmas born of conditions are from the first not the true nature. One should realize that although dharmas born of conditions take the nature as their essence, within the nature-essence there is no such birth from conditions, and so one should not cling to birth from conditions but be without it; that is the nature.

As for the non-nature of the supreme meaning: the nature of suchness is the essence of all dharmas; it is called the foremost meaning, also called the supreme meaning. This nature is real, inherently possessed by living beings, from the first complete — what is called perfect accomplishment. Yet the supreme meaning is also a name, just as hemp is also a provisional name. Hence it is called the non-nature of the supreme meaning: the supreme meaning too is a name and is not the nature. One should realize that within the nature of reality there is from the first no name of supreme meaning, and so one should not cling even to the supreme meaning but be without it; that is the nature of reality.

The nature school sets up its names somewhat differently. It calls the mark of no-mark the nature of no-mark, meaning that only when one does not cling to marks is it the true nature. It calls the non-nature of birth the nature of no-birth, meaning that only when one does not cling to birth from conditions is it the true nature. It calls the non-nature of the supreme meaning the nature of no-nature, meaning that only when one does not cling even to the nature is it the true nature. This meaning precisely shows that marks, being apart from the nature, have no substance, and the nature does not exist apart from marks either. In meaning it is all the more complete.

Therefore the nature of no-nature is also called the non-nature of truth, meaning that only when even the view of reality is absent is it the nature of reality. It is also called the non-nature of no-nature; the second no means empty, nothing — meaning that only when one does not cling to emptiness and nothingness is it the nature of reality.
The names and meanings have now been briefly explained. We should next take the simile of the dream to make clear the principle of the three natures and three non-natures.

The Buddha taught the three natures and three non-natures in order to reveal the interfusion of nature and marks. Those with wisdom should surely understand the principle of the three natures and three non-natures so as to penetrate both nature and marks; then they can be unattached to emptiness and existence alike and accord with the middle way.

And this sutra has us contemplate all conditioned dharmas as a dream because, by forming such a contemplation, one can penetrate the principle of the three natures and three non-natures. In other words: only one who understands the three natures and three non-natures can thoroughly comprehend that all conditioned dharmas are like a dream.

So now let us expound the meaning of being like a dream together with the meaning of the three natures and three non-natures, in the hope that both meanings may be thoroughly understood. As for the other five similes — illusion and the rest — they were originally spoken to prove the meaning of being like a dream. So although we speak here only of the dream, the meaning is already complete.

You should know that in the pure mind there are from the first no marks — this is called the nature of reality, just as when the mind is pure there are no dream-marks. But because the true nature follows conditions, it brings forth marks of body and mind (this means the deluded mind, that is, consciousness) and of the world. This is called the nature of dependence on others — no different from the marks of dream-realms that appear in accord with conditions when one falls asleep. Then ordinary people, not understanding that all conditioned dharmas are illusory marks born of conditions and that their birth is from the first no-birth, fall to reckoning and clinging, taking the unreal as real; this is called the nature of pervasive imagining. It is just as foolish folk, not knowing that the dream is an illusory mark born of conditions, existing yet not existing, cling to the dream-realm as real.
Therefore, if you know that the marks of dream-realms are all transformations of the one mind and that existing they do not exist, you should know that the nature of no-mark is likewise.

Now all dharmas are nothing but mind-made; hence they are called conditioned. Since conditioned dharmas are all mind-made, it is clear that the mind-nature is the true essence. All conditioned dharmas are merely marks that arise in accord with conditions by relying on the mind and leaning on events. That is why whatever has marks is illusory. How could one cling to them as real? To cling to them is to be deluded about marks and blind to the nature. Why? Because the nature is from the first without marks.

If you know that the mind has from the first no dream and that dreams arise only from the perfuming of deluded thought, and that deluded thought is itself unreal, so that the dreams it perfumes into being exist yet do not exist, then you should know that the nature of no-birth is likewise. Now all conditioned dharmas are marks of birth that falsely appear through the meeting of conditions; it is clear that within the nature-essence there is from the first no birth. Therefore all conditioned dharmas must not be clung to as real, and even their illusory marks born of conditions must not remain in the mind. If they remain, one is still blind to the nature. Why? Because the nature is not born of conditions.

If you know that the mind in dreaming and the mind awake are not two minds, but that because of sleep it is named the dream-mind, and that in truth apart from the dream-mind there is no separate waking mind, then you should know that the nature of no-nature is likewise. The deluded mind and the true mind are from the first non-dual; only because of ignorance and non-awakening is it named the deluded mind. If ignorance becomes clear and non-awakening becomes awakening, the deluded mind is the true mind — just as, if one does not fall asleep, the mind in dreaming is originally the waking mind. Therefore a cultivator must not, apart from the deluded mind, cling to a separate true mind. In other words, one should not annihilate form in order to reveal emptiness, nor annihilate marks in order to see the nature. To do so is still to be blind to the nature. Why? Because only in not clinging to the nature is there the nature of reality. And why is that? If there is any grasping, it becomes the mark of self and the view of self, and is no longer the mind of intrinsic purity.

What has been said above uses the meaning of being like a dream to explain the three natures and three non-natures; thus the meaning of the three natures and three non-natures is thoroughly illumined. And again it uses the meaning of the three natures and three non-natures to explain being like a dream; thus the meaning of being like a dream can also be thoroughly illumined. Reviewing what has been said about the three natures and three non-natures, one may know that the essential work lies only in not giving rise to pervasive imagining; then dependence on others is itself perfect accomplishment. Why? Because when one reckons and clings to neither nature nor marks, though marks blaze forth, the mind is from the first without marks; though one manifests entering birth and death, the nature is from the first without birth. Reckoning is discrimination, which is the sixth consciousness; clinging is the seventh consciousness. This is ignorance and non-awakening; this is the view of self.

Therefore the single main purport of this sutra lies in non-abiding, which is to break the self. Reviewing what has been said about being like a dream, one may know that the contemplation of dream goes through to the very end: from coarse to fine, from shallow to deep, from first cultivation to the ultimate. Every gate of practice is nothing but this contemplation. For the word dream is spoken to illustrate ignorance and non-awakening; and then the word like illustrates that ignorance and non-awakening seems to exist but is truly not, that the nature is from the first not existent. How exquisitely apt, how exactly true. Nor is that all: like a dream means seeming to dream. Seeming to dream precisely shows that all conditioned dharmas exist yet do not exist, and also shows that all conditioned dharmas do not exist yet do exist. Seeing that they exist yet do not exist, one must not cling to existence; seeing that they do not exist yet do exist, one must not cling to emptiness. So the words like a dream do not merely have us contemplate existence as a dream; they have us contemplate emptiness and existence alike as a dream. If one can truly see all conditioned dharmas as existing yet not existing, what hinders one from seeing all conditioned dharmas as not existing yet existing? This is called doing the Buddha's work in a dream on a grand scale. When a student first sets hand to the task and forms this perfect and sudden wondrous contemplation, then he clings neither to the real nor to the unreal, nor even to nothingness. This is what this sutra calls having no mark of self, no mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas — empty through and through. Then though he moves among existence, he does not abide in existence; though he practices emptiness, he does not abide in emptiness. Thus he can enter, in the middle of the middle, the true mark that is neither mark nor non-mark, and so be unmoving in suchness.

This is non-abiding while moving among existence and practicing emptiness, which is precisely the contemplation that is itself calm abiding. And moving among existence and emptiness while non-abiding is precisely the calm abiding that is itself contemplation. So to form such a contemplation is to practice calm abiding and contemplation together, and so to make concentration and wisdom equal. Attaining realization in this way, one can reach the still and ever-illumining, the illumining and ever-still — stillness and illumination at one and the same time. Hence it is said that all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.

In sum: the whole of the Diamond Prajñā, its wondrous purport of non-abiding, rests entirely on not grasping at marks, on being unmoving in suchness. And the way to reach not grasping at marks and being unmoving in suchness rests entirely on this: all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew, and like lightning — thus should they be contemplated. Every student should enter by following this contemplation. This contemplation is precisely the Diamond sword of wisdom, which nothing hard can resist and no ignorance or affliction can escape. Therefore one should expound it thus and uphold it thus, forever circulating this unsurpassed great Dharma that perpetuates the Buddha-seed.
(C) Next, the formal conclusion on circulating the sutra.

[When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, together with the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen, and all the worlds of gods, humans, asuras, and the rest, having heard what the Buddha said, were all greatly delighted, and they believed, accepted, honored, and practiced it.]

The words when the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra mean that this profoundly deep sutra had been spoken to the very end, with no meaning left unmanifest. The word finished answers precisely to the rejoicing and practicing that follow, showing that the capacities and the teaching met each other and that the great assembly was able to hear and to put it into practice. It also shows that believing, upholding, and transmitting it will go on forever without end: though it is called finished, in truth it was never finished.

The Elder is the one whose capacity the teaching met, and so he is listed first. Next are listed the four assemblies, all of them disciples of the Buddha's gate. The monks (which means mendicants, destroyers of evil, dreaded by Māra, and so on) and the nuns are the two orders of renunciates. The novices (a novice means one who rests in kindness, ceasing evil and practicing kindness, and is also called one diligent in the precepts) who have not yet received full ordination, and the novice nuns, are included as well. Laymen and laywomen are here rendered as pure-faith men and pure-faith women, also called male and female lay followers, meaning those who purify the three karmas and believe in and honor the path, and are fit to draw near the Three Jewels and to serve and make offerings to them. These are the two lay assemblies. A lay person who wishes to enter the Buddha's gate must first request a monk to confer the three refuges. If there is no monk, he may request a nun. This is formally entering the gate of the Three Jewels, and one may be called a disciple of the Buddha, also a disciple of the Three Jewels. When he then receives the five precepts he is called a layman or laywoman; without the five precepts he does not deserve the name. Going further, he may receive the bodhisattva precepts. Of the bodhisattva precepts, some are spoken universally for renunciates and lay people alike, such as the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts set out in the Brahmā Net Sutra; some are spoken specifically for the two lay assemblies, such as the six major and twenty-eight minor precepts set out in the Upāsaka Precepts Sutra. A lay person who examines himself and finds he can keep them one by one as a renunciate does may receive them together with renunciates; otherwise he had better receive the six major and twenty-eight minor. For once the precepts are received they must be upheld; if one receives them and does not uphold them, the offense is not small. One must weigh the matter carefully before receiving them. After receiving the bodhisattva precepts, one is called a bodhisattva-precept layman or laywoman. If one has not yet taken the three refuges formally, one is called only a faithful man or faithful woman, not a disciple of the Buddha, nor a layman or laywoman. Laymen and laywomen may all expound sutras and teach the Dharma and be Dharma masters; only they may not be masters of refuge and precepts, because they have not themselves received full ordination. The three refuges are themselves precepts. Nowadays there are those who seek refuge from a lay spiritual friend — this is a mistake. You should know that to seek refuge is to seek the transmission of the three refuges as precepts; this may be sought only from a renunciate spiritual friend. If one seeks from a lay spiritual friend instruction in sutras and Dharma, becoming his student and taking him as teacher, there is certainly no objection; and if that person's vow is sincere and he is fit to teach, the spiritual friend likewise should not simply refuse him harshly. Whether in a gathering place or on the road, the two lay assemblies should respectfully yield and let renunciates go first. Though renunciates and lay people are alike children of the Buddha, in terms of order the monk is like the eldest son, and after him come the nun, the novice, the novice nun, the layman, and the laywoman — the order must not be confused.

You should know that renunciates have cut off affection, left the dust of the world behind, and already stand among those who uphold the Three Jewels; how could the two lay assemblies, mired in the five desires and trailing mud and water, compare with them? Therefore they should be respected. Even a monk who breaks the precepts must not be slighted. Why? You should know that the precepts of renunciation are numerous, dense, and grave: a monk's full ordination has two hundred and fifty rules; a nun's full ordination has more than three hundred and seventy. With a moment's heedlessness one has already transgressed. The word upholding is easily said, but how hard it is. Even novices and novice nuns receive ten precepts, twice as many as lay people. How can one lightly ridicule them? If one truly knows that their words and conduct contradict each other, or that they fail to keep the pure rules, one may respect them from afar — this follows the Buddha's institution, what is called silent censure. Silent means not proclaiming their faults; censure means keeping one's distance. The same applies to lay people whose words and conduct contradict each other. This is the duty a cultivator should keep, and it must not be neglected.

In sum, if the Buddha-Dharma is to flourish, there must be, among both renunciates and lay people, those of lofty practice and weighty virtue whom the many accept, to serve as leaders; and the government must be clear and bright, with the principal men in it also able to believe in the Three Jewels, so that protecting and ordering one another, it may at last succeed. By the Buddha's institution, if a renunciate transgresses the Buddha-Dharma, the matter goes to the leading elders of the Saṅgha, who judge it by the Buddha's Vinaya. If he also breaks the laws of the state, then with the consent of those leading elders he must first be unfrocked, and only afterwards may he be judged by worldly law. And above all, at the time of tonsure and ordination the qualifications must be strictly chosen: this is the way to rectify the root and purify the source.

The Sahā world is one great trichiliocosm. Within it there are a billion four-continent worlds, a billion heavens of the six desires, and so on. Moreover, when the Buddha spoke the Dharma, bodhisattvas, gods, dragons, and others from countless worlds in the ten directions came to the assembly — very many indeed. Hence it says all the worlds. To speak of gods and asuras is to include the eight classes. The word humans here refers generally to those beyond the four assemblies. That bodhisattvas are not mentioned has two meanings. First, this sutra was spoken at the ninth assembly of the great prajñā gathering, and bodhisattvas were already listed in full at the earlier assemblies, so they are omitted here. Second, this sutra is spoken for those who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna, who have resolved upon the supreme vehicle; one may see that all present in the assembly were bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas who had resolved upon the unsurpassed bodhi mind, and so they are not listed separately.

That they were all greatly delighted means that hearing this great Dharma their minds opened and their understanding was released — this is delight. And knowing that to believe, accept, honor, and practice it is to shoulder the Tathāgata's burden, that they would attain bodhi and have hope of Buddhahood, which is no small matter — therefore they were greatly delighted. Every one of the assembly was like this, and so all were greatly delighted.

Faith means the faith whose mind does not oppose; acceptance means understanding, the understanding that deeply comprehends the purport. Because they had the faith that does not oppose and the acceptance that deeply comprehends, they therefore honored and practiced it. To honor means to revere and follow, that is, to follow the purport set out in the sutra. The word practice covers both benefiting oneself and benefiting others: having honored and practiced it oneself, one further spreads this sutra abroad and expounds it for others, causing all living beings to be without exception greatly delighted. Thus to believe and accept, thus to honor and practice — one must let the water of wisdom flow on forever and the lineage of Dharma be forever unobstructed, transmitted through dust-calendar aeons without stagnation, reaching all kinds of beings without omission. Then throughout the Dharma-realm and to the end of time, wherever this sutra is, there is where the Buddha speaks the Dharma. The earlier phrase when the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra is spoken only with respect to the circumstances of one time. The compilers' intent was that the whole great assembly would practice according to the teaching and the Buddha-seed would never be cut off; and so our World-Honored One's speaking of this sutra in truth has no time of finishing at all. Not only did those who compiled this sutra possess this vast vow: we today who speak it, who hear it, who initiate this Dharma assembly and who sustain it, are likewise all greatly delighted, believing, accepting, honoring, and practicing it, and share this same vow. To possess this vow is truly to believe and accept, truly to honor and practice, truly to rejoice. Herein precisely do we repay the Buddha's kindness. I, unwise, am ashamed that in this deep sutra I have not fulfilled the measure of its exposition; I have but spoken one drop of the great ocean. Yet even this one drop already holds the taste of the whole sea. I only pray that all spiritual friends may enter from true faith into pure faith, and from the conditioned realize the unconditioned, adorning the Buddha-lands with these practices and vows and converting living beings; then one may become a Buddha in this very body — how much more than merely being assured of birth in the West.

blocks.text: 1. Collation Notes on the Diamond Sutra

inline.s: This edition follows throughout the Tang dynasty manuscript from the Dunhuang stone chamber, and the text written by Liu Gongquan is one of the scriptures hidden in that chamber. Photographic reprints have long circulated in the world and can be checked against it. Therefore in the collation notes Liu's text is listed first, and the various texts consulted for comparison follow. I shall now set out in full, before the collation notes, the name of each edition relied upon and whether a separate edition of it circulates, so that checking may be easy.

The colophon after Liu's text reads: On the sixth day of the fourth month of the fourth year of Changqing, the court gentleman Liu Gongquan wrote it out for the monk-registrar Zhun of the Right Street. As to Liu's text: during the Xuantong reign of the Qing, the Youzheng Book Company of Shanghai gathered more than ten items from the stone chamber's holdings and reproduced them in collotype under the title Secret Treasures of the Stone Chamber. Liu's text is one of those treasures. Changqing is the reign title of Emperor Muzong of Tang.

Weng's text: the fifty-seventh year of the Qianlong reign, cyclical year renzi. Written out by Weng Fanggang. His colophon reads: followed the stone text of Dharma Master Daoyong of the Southern Tang. As Weng's text follows a Five Dynasties stone engraving of the Southern Tang, it is listed before the Song canon. A lithographic gift edition presently exists.

The Song canon: printed at the Qisha Yansheng Monastery of Pingjiang Prefecture in the Shaoding reign of Emperor Lizong of the Southern Song — the so-called Qisha canon. This canon was begun in the fourth year of Shaoding and completed in the second year of Zhida of Emperor Wuzong of Yuan, eighty years from first to last before the work was finished. It was originally kept at the Wolong and Kaiyuan monasteries in Xi'an, and later moved to the Shaanxi Provincial Library. The Shanghai Society for the Photographic Reproduction of the Song Edition of the Canon is at present reproducing it.

Zhang's text: the second year of Baoyou of Emperor Lizong of the Southern Song, cyclical year jiayin. Written out by Zhang Chuliao, that is, Zhang Jizhi. His own colophon reads: followed the edition collated by the Tiantai teaching monk Zongyin. In the fourth year of Kangxi of the Qing, cyclical year yisi, Da Chongguang and others traced and engraved it on stone for the Shibi Hut at Mount Jiao. Note that the second year of Baoyou is more than twenty years after Shaoding. Its sentences differ slightly from the Qisha canon. Rubbings exist. There is also a lithographic gift edition written out by Wang Daxie in the seventeenth year of the Republic, following Zhang's text.

The Diamond Sutra with Commentary and Subcommentary, annotated by the monk Huijing of Jiguo Monastery of the Tang. Before the commentary stands a preface by Chu Liang of Henan, erudite of the Changtai Hall of the Tang, a contemporary of Master Hui. After it comes a colophon by the Japanese Sanyin of Danyang, which says in brief: this commentary did not circulate in China, nor was it seen in Japan. Recently Master Yikong obtained the true text and published it for lasting transmission. A treasure long hidden has in one morning shone forth its radiance — one may say it has met its time. Early autumn of the second year of Xiangbao, cyclical year dingyou. Note that the Japanese Xiangbao dingyou is the fifty-sixth year of Kangxi of our Qing. When the sutra text was incorporated is unclear. Collated against Liu's text, the words and sentences largely agree, and it lacks one passage of the Wei translation; it must precede the other combined editions, and so it is listed first.

The Diamond Sutra with Commentary, annotated by the monk Sengzhao of the Later Qin. It has a preface by the Japanese monk Jingxiong, which says: long ago it was brought back from China by the Great Master Cijue, and was kept secret in famous mountains for nine hundred years. Recently the Chan man Zufang brought it out to show me. I sighed and said: among commentaries on this sutra, Master Zhao's comes first; among commentaries that came to the East, this one also came first; and that it has appeared after all the other commentaries were already in circulation — is this not a matter of time and conditions? The Great Master of Tiantai once lectured on this sutra relying solely on Master Zhao, just as in expounding the Contemplation Sutra he relied solely on Jingying. If it is cut and circulated, how great will its benefit be? Summer of the twelfth year of Baoli, cyclical year renwu. Note that the Japanese Baoli renwu is the twenty-seventh year of Qianlong of our Qing, one hundred and seventy-two years ago. Going back nine hundred years from that puts it about the beginning of the Xiantong reign of Emperor Yizong, late in our Tang. When the sutra text was incorporated is likewise unknown. It differs here and there from the Southern Tang stone engraving and the Changshui Record of Definitive Editing. It has also added the sixty-two characters of the Wei translation, with a note beneath them saying: these sixty-two characters are absent from Zhao's text, and the Tiantai subcommentary has no sectioning either; but since all other texts have this passage, it is retained here. So one may know that it must be later than the combined edition of Hui's commentary. The two books above are both found in the Continuation of the Canon reproduced by the Commercial Press, and have no separate editions. (Gu Nong notes: the copy in the Continuation of the Canon was once engraved at the Ganzhou Sutra-Engraving Office in the ninth year of the Republic by Ding Weisen and others, following the edition collated by Li Duanfu.)
Master Zhiyi's Subcommentary on the Diamond Sutra, spoken by Zhiyi of Tiantai of the Sui; engraved at Jinling in the thirty-third year of Guangxu of the Qing.
The Meaning Subcommentary on the Diamond Sutra, composed by Jizang of Jiaxiang of the Sui; engraved at Jinling in the sixth year of the Republic.
The Praising Exposition of the Diamond Sutra, composed by Kuiji of the Great Ci'en Monastery of the Tang; engraved at Jinling in the sixth year of the Republic.

The Essential Compilation of Subcommentaries and Treatises on the Diamond Sutra, set forth by Zongmi of the Great Xingfu Monastery of the Tang; engraved at Beiping in the eleventh year of the Republic. Note that the four books above were all obtained from Japan. The Meaning Subcommentary originally had no sutra text; the text was incorporated when it was engraved at Jinling, and so it agrees with the presently circulating edition. The sutra text incorporated into the other three books either follows their old form or does not follow it in full, and so they agree with the circulating edition in some places and differ in others. The separate editions can be collated against the Continuation of the Canon.

The Combined Subcommentary and Record on the Diamond Sutra, engraved at Beiping in the nineteenth year of the Republic. The subcommentary is the Essential Compilation of Subcommentaries and Treatises; the record is the Record of Definitive Editing composed by the monk Zixuan of Changshui in the Song. Note that the Continuation of the Canon contains the sectional combination of subcommentary and record by the Ming monk Dabing, recut in the forty-seventh year of Qianlong of the Qing after an old Yunqi edition; by it one may examine how the sutra text of Ming times differed from the present edition.
Collation Notes
How should one abide?

(Identical in Liu's text, Weng's text, the Song canon, Zhang's text, the Ming engraving, and Hui's, Zhao's, and the Essential Compilation and three combined editions. The presently circulating edition and the early Qing edition read: how should one abide, agreeing with the wording of the Later Zhou. Note that the Praising Exposition, in quoting the sutra, also reads how should one abide.)
If not having thought, and not without thought.

(Identical in Liu's text and down to the Ming engraving, and in Hui's commentary, Zhao's commentary, Zhi's subcommentary, the Praising Exposition, the Essential Compilation, the five combined editions, and the present circulating edition. In early Qing engraved editions some add the character if before not without thought, noting: the ancient texts do not have it. Note that since the ancient texts do not have it, how could it be added indiscriminately? Collating all the editions I have seen, it appears that from late Tang onward the sutra text was successively enlarged and altered by people, and that the most additions and alterations were made between the Ming and Qing.)
If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, then he is not a bodhisattva.
(In Zhao's combined edition the two characters bodhisattva are absent after if; all other editions have them.)
Then one sees the Tathāgata.

(Identical in Liu's text, Weng's text, the Song canon, Zhang's text, and Hui's, Zhao's, and Zhi's subcommentary and the three combined editions. The circulating edition reads then as that is. So do all Ming and Qing engravings.)
On these chapter phrases.
(All editions ancient and modern agree. Only Zhao's combined edition reads: these on the chapter phrases.)
Then one clings to self, person, being, and life.
(All editions ancient and modern agree. Only the early Qing engraving reads that is for then.)
Why? If one grasps the mark of non-Dharma.
(All editions ancient and modern agree. In the early Qing engraving some suspected the three characters why is that to be a redundant addition and deleted them.)
Therefore the Tathāgata speaks of the abundance of merit. If again there be one.
(All editions ancient and modern agree. In early Qing there is an engraving that adds the five characters the Buddha said, Subhūti before if again.)
What are called Buddhadharmas are then not Buddhadharmas.

(All editions ancient and modern agree. In early Qing there is an edition that adds the sentence this is named Buddhadharma after the clause then not. Note that the Changshui Record of Definitive Editing says: as in the sutra, then not Buddhadharma is the supreme meaning, blocking the extreme of addition; this is named Buddhadharma is the worldly meaning, blocking the extreme of subtraction; the rest of the then not and this is named follow this pattern — see the Combined Subcommentary and Record, juan 3, page 11. So at Changshui's time there was already an engraved edition, and it is unknown who added this sentence. Yet examining the purport of Guifeng's subcommentary, there is in fact no this is named sentence. The subcommentary says: in the foremost meaning there is no Buddhadharma that comes forth from the sutra — see the Essential Compilation, upper juan, page 26. The Changshui Record, on this point, explains according to the subcommentary and does not reach the this is named sentence — see the Combined Compilation, juan 4, page 32. Examining the commentaries and subcommentaries of the ancient worthies, none of them has the meaning of a this is named sentence.)
Yet in truth he does not come.

(Identical in Liu's text, the Song canon, and Hui's text. The circulating edition reads: yet in truth he does not not-come; the Southern Tang stone engraving had already added the character not. Note that Zhi's subcommentary and Jizang's Meaning Subcommentary both say: by not is also included not. Hui's commentary says: since in contemplation one does not see a self, who is there to speak of as not coming? Hence it says yet in truth he does not come. This is sufficient proof that the original reads does not come.)
He is the foremost Arhat free from desire; I do not conceive such a thought.

(Identical in Liu's text and down to the Ming engraving, and in Hui's commentary and the other five combined editions. The circulating edition has the two characters World-Honored One before I. So do all early Qing editions.)
If I were to conceive such a thought.
(All editions ancient and modern agree. Only Zhao's text lacks the character I.)
Does he obtain any Dharma? No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
(Identical in Liu's text and Hui's text. In the circulating edition the two characters no indeed follow does he obtain any. So do all editions from the Southern Tang stone engraving onward.)
Then it is not adornment.
(Identical in Liu's text, the Song canon, Zhang's text, and Hui's text. The circulating edition reads that is not. So do the Southern Tang stone engraving and all Ming and Qing editions.)
But this merit surpasses that former merit.
(All editions ancient and modern agree. Only Hui's text reads like for but.)
Then there is a Buddha.

(Identical in Liu's text and down to the Ming engraving, and in Hui's commentary, the Essential Compilation, and the two combined editions. In the circulating edition and all early Qing editions, then reads that is.)
Then it is not prajñā-pāramitā.

(Identical in Liu's text and down to the Ming engraving, and in Hui's combined edition. In the circulating edition and all early Qing editions, then reads that is, and there further follows the sentence this is named prajñā-pāramitā. In early Qing there is an edition that also notes beneath it: the ancient texts do not have it. Note that the sentence this is named prajñā-pāramitā is first seen added in the Southern Song Qisha canon; it is absent not only from the Tang manuscript but also from the Southern Tang stone engraving and Zhang Chuliao's text. The sutra text of Hui's commentary and the other five combined editions all lack the this is named sentence. Further, examining Zhao's commentary: then not prajñā is itself the emptiness of wisdom; when the object is extinguished the wisdom is forgotten, and what mark is not exhausted? The purport of spreading and upholding should lie herein. Zhi's subcommentary agrees. Zhi's subcommentary also says: prajñā is then not prajñā — this is like emptiness. Jizang's Meaning Subcommentary says: prajñā is not prajñā, the mind's activity is cut off; below, the Tathāgata teaches nothing, cutting off words and speech. It also says: the Buddha speaks of prajñā — this is the Buddha's prajñā; then not prajñā — this is not the wisdom of the two vehicles. Hui's commentary says: on the day one realizes the truth one obtains true prajñā; when one obtains the truth one then relinquishes words, and so it says the Buddha speaks of prajñā, then not prajñā. The Praising Exposition says: then it is not prajñā-pāramitā — this is not something one Buddha alone set forth. The Essential Compilation says: then not prajñā — as Asaṅga says, this is to counter the clinging that follows words. None of the ancient commentaries above explains the this is named.)
May one see the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One. Why?

(Identical in Liu's text and Hui's text. In the circulating edition the sentence one may not see the Tathāgata by the thirty-two marks stands before why. Note that the Southern Tang stone engraving had already added this sentence. Examining the ancient commentaries, none of them explains it. The Meaning Subcommentary holds that it still serves to explain and complete the preceding meaning of may one see the Tathāgata by the bodily marks, and so it is explained in a continuous thread with the preceding text.)
Then the true mark is produced.
(All editions ancient and modern agree; the early Qing edition reads that is for then.)
Then it is not a mark.
(Identical in Liu's text and down to the Ming engraving, and in Hui's commentary and the other five combined editions. In the circulating edition and the early Qing edition, then reads that is.)
